posts.text:
Your Amazon PPC report shows more orders. But did it show more units—or more profit?

An order is a transaction. Units sold measure product volume. Mixing them up can distort decisions about PPC scaling, replenishment, and actual demand.

Consider an illustrative campaign comparison:

Period A: 100 orders, 125 units, $1,000 spend.
Period B: 110 orders, 112 units, $1,200 spend.

Orders increased by 10%, yet units declined by 10.4% while advertising spend increased by 20%. Calling Period B an improvement based on order count alone would be misleading.

For a stronger PPC diagnosis, I track:
1. Units sold alongside orders and units per order.
2. Spend per unit and ad-attributed contribution margin.
3. Search-term intent and placement changes.
4. Conversion rate on comparable traffic—not blended averages alone.
5. Organic and paid sales together to assess whether growth is incremental.

The goal is not simply more clicks or a better-looking dashboard. It is profitable unit velocity.

When evaluating a campaign, which metric do you prioritize: orders, units sold, or contribution profit?

AI automation fails when success is defined as simply completing a workflow.

Before deploying an agent to handle operational work, I define its measurable output, accessible evidence, allowed tool calls, and escalation conditions.

Four checks matter:
• Did the system choose the correct action?
• Was the underlying data current and trustworthy?
• Can the result be verified independently?
• What is the cost of reaching that result?

Automating the boring work is valuable. Automating an unchecked decision just scales uncertainty.

Which business process would you automate first—and how would you verify the result?

#AIAgents #LLM #AIAutomation #AIEngineering #AppliedAI

More Amazon PPC spend does not automatically mean more profitable demand.

The reel explains a common optimization mistake: treating additional clicks as evidence of growth.

I prefer to compare units per click, search-term intent, conversion rate, placement mix, and contribution margin before increasing bids.

If clicks rise but units stay flat, the bottleneck may be traffic quality or listing conversion—not insufficient spend.

Would you increase bids before reviewing search-term conversion?
